title: Five pillars, one house
hook: the pillars hold up a life the way the prayer hall's columns hold the roof

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hajj of the heart, and your line: longing counts. What good thing can't you do yet, and what small piece of it did you do from where you are? Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

A prayer hall has a carpet, light from the windows, a niche that points toward Mecca. And it has columns. They stand there, row after row, doing their one job, and the roof stays up. A column is easy to overlook until it's missing. That's the picture behind a report the Prophet's companions passed on, one that turns religion into architecture. Today, the five pillars, and the house they hold up.
screen: `EASY TO OVERLOOK.` → `ROW AFTER ROW, ONE JOB.` → `RELIGION AS ARCHITECTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the report. Abdullah ibn Umar relates, in Sahih Muslim, that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: Islam is built upon five. Testifying that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His messenger. Establishing the prayer. Giving zakat. Fasting Ramadan. And the Hajj. Notice the verb. Not ruled by five, not summed up in five. Built. Islam is described as a building. Second, how carefully it was kept. In the same collection, a man repeats the list back to Ibn Umar and puts the Hajj before the fast. Ibn Umar stops him: no, fasting Ramadan and then the Hajj, that is how I heard it from the Messenger of God. A small correction, and it shows how closely Ibn Umar held to the exact words. Third, look back. This block walked through the building one pillar at a time. The testimony, two sentences. The prayer, its times and its stillness. Zakat, the share that purifies. The fast, its shield and its two joys. And these last weeks, the pilgrimage, from the boundary and the two white cloths, to Arafah and Muzdalifah, the stones, the sacrifice, the haircut, the circlings, and the longing of those who stay home. Fourth, why one house and not five separate rules. The pillars hold the same roof. They also bend to the person under it. Zakat falls on those with wealth, the fast has its exemptions, the Hajj is due only on those who are able. The building is drawn to fit the people who live in it. One house, five columns, and a roof over a whole life.
screen: `ISLAM IS BUILT UPON FIVE.` · `IBN UMAR KEPT THE ORDER.` · `ONE PILLAR AT A TIME.` · `ONE ROOF, SHARED WEIGHT.` · then, large: `FIVE PILLARS, ONE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: name the pillar you're strongest in. Settle, and breathe. Go through them slowly, the way you'd walk past columns in a hall. The testimony. The prayer. Giving. The fast. The pilgrimage, or the longing for it. If you're learning about Islam rather than practicing it, ask the same question in your own life: which of your daily supports is steadiest? Rest your attention on that one. Don't rush to the weak one yet. That's tomorrow. If you pray, you can thank God for what's holding. The bell holds the time.
Five pillars. The testimony, the prayer, zakat, the fast of Ramadan and the Hajj: in Ibn Umar's report, the five Islam is built upon. Today's word.

Your line: five pillars, one house. This week took you from the haircut at Mina to the circlings, the farewell, Medina, and the longing at home. Today, lean on your strongest pillar once, on purpose. Tomorrow: the weakest pillar. Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims learn the five pillars, the testimony, prayer, zakat, the fast of Ramadan and the Hajj, from the report of Ibn Umar, and some teachers present them as the supports of one building.

notes: Bukhari 8 (Ibn Umar): 'Islam is built upon five'. In Bukhari's wording the Hajj is listed before the fast; the script lists the five in that order in the teach, then reports Muslim 16, where Ibn Umar corrects a man to 'fasting Ramadan and the Hajj'. A Keeper may want this tension acknowledged or the teach's list reordered.

Week-end look-back (1135–1141) in the carry; block look-back (1063–1140) in the teach. Short labels for earlier days ('the share that purifies', 'its shield and its two joys') echo earlier lessons' carries; confirm they match.
'Zakat falls on those with wealth' simplifies nisab; confirm.
Prayer-hall columns image is the outline's own; the niche (mihrab) description is general.
Practice invites thanks 'if you pray'; no new prayer written.

Editor: resolved the order tension in the first note: the teach now cites Muslim 16 for the list, in the fast-then-Hajj order Ibn Umar insists on, so the correction that follows is consistent; hook no longer claims 'nobody' looks at the columns; 'the companions held the exact words' narrowed to Ibn Umar (teach and myth); cut the narrator's 'a column that can't carry its weight doesn't bring the house down' theology; 'several columns' made 'five'.
